characters: Ntow: a 10-year-old boy in a school uniform, with a plastic bottle and a pencil.
Mamle: his classmate, 10, in a school uniform, who remembers swimming in the river.
Mr Appiah: their science teacher, in a blue shirt, holding two clear jars.
The river: a wide river that is clear in one picture and thick brown in the next, with a water plant on the bank (story picture).
music: Gentle flowing water becoming heavy and slow; a hopeful tune at the end (placeholder)
culturalNotes: This is a science story set in an invented school beside an invented river. The facts come from published reports named in the fact-check.
Not all mud in rivers comes from galamsey; the story names other causes too.
The numbers about turbidity differ between sources and the story says so.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: turbidity of 5,000 to 12,000 NTU against a normal 0 to 500 (a minister, February 2025) versus above 10,000 NTU (a commentary); GWCL plant shutdowns including Daboase and Kyebi; a CSIR researcher’s claim that over 60 per cent of water bodies are polluted; rivers named (Pra, Ankobra, Birim, Offin); recovery estimate of 10 to 20 years (an editorial).
Confirm the safe NTU range with the Ghana Water Company or the Water Resources Commission before release.
Check that the home-filter activity is described as a demonstration only, not as a way to make river water safe to drink.

teacherGuide.overview: A science story that introduces turbidity, links galamsey to muddy rivers and water supply, and shows that prevention beats cure. It teaches careful reading of figures that differ.
learningGoals: Explain turbidity and how it is measured.
Describe how muddy rivers affect water plants, fish and people.
Explain why a home filter does not make river water safe.
beforeReading: Fill two jars, one with clean water and one with muddy water, and ask learners which is safe to drink and why.
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to compare 500 with 5,000 and 12,000.
afterReading: Make a bottle filter as a demonstration. Do not drink the water.
Draw a river with healthy banks.
discussion: Why do figures sometimes differ between reports?
What can a community do to protect its river banks?
reflection: What would you like your river to look like in twenty years?

mathsExtension.task: Normal water is up to 500 NTU. A river has 5,000 NTU. How many times higher is it?
A river has 12,000 NTU. How many times higher than 500?

support: Provide a picture scale with green, yellow and red zones.
stretch: Design a way to measure how muddy a stream is using a clear tube and a marked disc.

culturalNotes: This is a science story set in an invented school beside an invented river. The facts come from published reports named in the fact-check.
Not all mud in rivers comes from galamsey; the story names other causes too.
The numbers about turbidity differ between sources and the story says so.
localiseThis: Use your nearest river or stream; invite a water company or environmental officer.
Never let learners enter rivers; do the activity at school with an adult.

whatWeKnow: Illegal mining has made several rivers very muddy.
Water plants have shut down when water was too muddy to treat.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The exact share of polluted water bodies.
How long it will take rivers to recover.

factCheck.claim: Water turbidity of 5,000 to 12,000 NTU against a normal range of 0 to 500; 44 of 288 forest reserves face serious threats from illegal mining.
factCheck.explanation: Reported from a minister’s statement at a conference.
factCheck.reference: Ghana News Agency, “Ghana’s cocoa farms under siege” (27 February 2025).

factCheck.claim: More than 60 per cent of Ghana’s water bodies are polluted by illegal mining (a researcher’s statement); rivers affected include the Pra, Ankobra, Birim, Offin and Densu; the Ghana Water Company has repeatedly shut plants including at Daboase and Kyebi; recovery may take 10 to 20 years (an estimate).
factCheck.explanation: From a Daily Graphic editorial of 12 August 2026, which is opinion.
factCheck.reference: Graphic Online, “Can Ghana heal her water?”.

factCheck.claim: Turbidity at some intakes above 10,000 NTU, about five times the treatable level; plants reduced output or shut; higher treatment costs.
factCheck.explanation: From an opinion column that cites reports without providing them.

narrationPlan.voice: Curious young voices for Ntow and Mamle; calm, encouraging voice for Mr Appiah
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and clear, slower at the muddy water (about 115 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.
